profiles.name: Alexander Scott
profiles.description: Alexander Scott was the editor of the Passaic Weekly Issue, a socialist newspaper that covered the 1913 Paterson silk strike sympathetically. He was prosecuted under New Jersey's 1902 Criminal Anarchy Law — passed after the McKinley assassination — for editorials condemning Paterson police violence against strikers. Sentenced to 1 to 15 years at the New Jersey State Prison in Trenton, his case became a landmark First Amendment fight for the early labor and free-speech movements.

profiles.name: George Bradley
profiles.description:
George Bradley was reportedly secretary of the Everett IWW local for only one day before local authorities or vigilantes expelled him from Everett. He was arrested in Seattle on September 29, 1916, in parallel with James Johnson, transported to Everett and accused of participating in a second-degree arson conspiracy. Police reportedly attempted to induce confessions by falsely telling each man the other had confessed — though the two had allegedly never met before their arrests — a detail that strongly suggests a frame-up connected to the wider campaign against the Everett IWW. Bradley was released with Johnson on November 23, 1916; no conviction or sentence was imposed.

He should not be automatically identified with any similarly named person in the post-Everett Massacre prisoner photographs.

profiles.name: Henry H. Franz
profiles.description: Henry H. Franz was a Mennonite Brethren conscientious objector who died at age 22 while imprisoned at the Fort Leavenworth military prison. Born near Inman, Kansas to Henry and Agnes Franz, Russian-German immigrants, he was farming near Hooker, Oklahoma when he registered for the draft in June 1917, claiming exemption on "Mennonite conviction." Court-martialed at Camp Travis with a group of 45 conscientious objectors — all sentenced to life imprisonment, later reduced to 25 years, for refusing to wear the uniform — he was transferred to the Fort Leavenworth disciplinary barracks in June 1918. Weakened by the brutal treatment of objectors (solitary confinement, bread-and-water diets, stress positions) and vulnerable to the 1918 influenza pandemic, he died in custody on December 1, 1918, three weeks after the Armistice, while awaiting the release that came too late. He is buried in the Adams Mennonite Brethren Cemetery near Adams, Oklahoma. (He is often incorrectly listed as "Henry E. Franz.")

profiles.name: James Johnson
profiles.description:
James Johnson was arrested in Seattle on September 29, 1916, as Everett authorities attempted to build an arson conspiracy case against IWW members in the conflict that preceded the Everett Massacre. He was taken to the Everett jail and accused of involvement in local fires. Walker C. Smith's contemporary account says Johnson was initially held without a warrant — one was not issued until October 17, about nineteen days after the arrest — and that authorities shifted their theory when one of the fires attributed to him turned out to have occurred after he was already in custody. Police reportedly tried to induce confessions by falsely telling Johnson and his co-accused George Bradley that the other had confessed, though the two had allegedly never met before their arrests. Smith reported that Johnson was jailed fifty-eight days without a preliminary hearing; the calendar interval from September 29 to the November 23 release is fifty-five days, so one of the dates or the count is imprecise, and the fifty-eight-day figure is kept as reported rather than as arithmetic.

He is not the J. J. Johnson of the Los Angeles criminal-syndicalism records, nor any other James Johnson in this database.

profiles.finding: UW IWW booking inventory corroborates detention but selected original individual portrait not retrieved. Everett Public Library originals remain a lead.

profiles.name: James Schmidt
profiles.description: James Schmidt was an itinerant IWW member prosecuted at Aberdeen, South Dakota in 1915 for killing a railroad brakeman. By the defense account reported in labor and later scholarly sources, the brakeman attempted to extort money from Schmidt and then threatened or tried to shoot him; Schmidt maintained he acted in self-defense. The case went to trial, the jury failed to reach a verdict — a majority reportedly favoring acquittal on self-defense grounds — and Schmidt remained confined for a little more than a year while prosecutors considered a retrial. The charge was dismissed on October 7, 1916 and he was released. Descriptions of the case as dismissed "without trial" are misleading: there was a trial, it ended without a verdict, and no retrial followed. The exact institution of his custody is unresolved.

profiles.name: Max Dezettel
profiles.description:
Max Dezettel was a Spokane IWW organizer and local secretary who went to Boise, Idaho in August 1911 to establish or assist an IWW local and was arrested after attempting to speak publicly. One report said police choked and struck him while taking him to jail. The Industrial Worker reported that he was denied the opportunity to defend himself and sentenced to fifty days, but a follow-up report said he was released after about four days, after ostensibly promising not to speak again — only to resume speaking shortly afterward. The sentence was evidently suspended, shortened or not fully served; the surviving reports do not explain the legal mechanism.

He later worked in syndicalist and labor publishing, associated with the Kansas City paper The Toiler alongside Earl Browder and with plans for a Chicago labor publication connected to the Trade Union Educational League.

Court-martialed for refusing military service, he was held at Fort Leavenworth. (Documented in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection's World War I Conscientious Objectors database.) Archival note: joined the Church of the Brethren at the age of twelve; sent to Camp Greenleaf; refused uniform, until forced upon him; refused to drill; worked in camp; after release from Leavenworth, was sent to Ft. profiles.name: Thomas Savage
profiles.description: Thomas Savage was one of the 74 Industrial Workers of the World members held in the Snohomish County jail and charged with murder after the Everett Massacre. On November 5, 1916, some 300 Industrial Workers of the World members sailed from Seattle to Everett, Washington aboard the steamers Verona and Calista to support a shingle-weavers' strike and the IWW's free-speech fight. At the Everett dock, Snohomish County sheriff Donald McRae and a posse of armed vigilantes opened fire on the Verona, killing at least five Wobblies and wounding dozens. The returning IWW members were arrested, and 74 were charged with the murder of two deputies (Jefferson Beard and Charles Curtis) killed in the gunfire. Only Thomas H. Tracy was brought to trial; after his acquittal on May 5, 1917, the charges against the others were dropped. At the time of the massacre he was 50, a machinist, born in New York.

profiles.name: Walter Schols
profiles.description: Walter Schols was prosecuted under United States wartime statutes of the World War I era (chiefly the Espionage Act, the Sedition Act, or the Selective Service Act). Recorded offense: Conspiracy. Sentence: Four years in. Sentenced May 9, 1916. Later disposition: Sentence commuted. This case is documented in the 1921 U.S. Senate hearing "Amnesty and Pardon for Political Prisoners" (digitized by the Internet Archive).

profiles.name: William Weyh
profiles.description: William Weyh was an IWW leader. William Weyh was convicted of seditious conspiracy at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to five years and fined $20,000. He began his term in Leavenworth Penitentiary on September 7, 1918. Weyh contracted tuberculosis at Leavenworth. Despite his tuberculin condition, he was forced to perform hard labor (breaking rocks) until he suffered twelve hemorrhages in a single day. On December 27, 1921, the prison physician notified Warden W. I. Biddle that Weyh's condition was terminal: "He has had several veiy severe pulmonary hemorrhages in the past few days and the case is very liable to terminate fatally at any time." Even this did not persuade the Department of Justice, which refused to pardon Weyh. According to IWW prisoners: [After his December hemorrhages] he was so emaciated as to be scarcely recognizable. It was at this point that a prison official said to him: "I don't believe you have another ten hours to live if you stay in this place. Drop your I.W.W. affiliations, and you can be out of here." Weyh's answer was: "No, I'll die first." Weyh continued to suffer in jail for another year until he agreed to the Department of Justice's demand that he be deported if his tuberculosis was cured. Weyh was released on January 25, 1922, but never recuperated and died from tuberculosis two years later, on March 22, 1924.
